verdict.root_cause: Every sampled PlaceOrder trace terminates at checkoutservice's CartService/GetCart span with ERROR status, which propagates up through checkoutservice PlaceOrder to the frontend HTTP POST [tr_6b9848cec352]. The spans complete in 2-5ms with no accumulated latency, so cartservice is returning an immediate error rather than hanging. checkoutservice itself is healthy on everything measured: it keeps accepting orders, logs no errors, and never crashes [tr_ba4ec2f0c565], and has no self-time in its spans [tr_6b9848cec352]. Its errors are new versus a two-hour baseline but bursty and partial, with three separate threshold crossings at 00:51, 01:20 and 02:12 rather than a single cutover [tr_3c5dd3f3ddbc]. Frontend is only the caller [tr_9d797b72def0]. I blame cartservice: it is rejecting GetCart calls fast and intermittently, a shape that fits a capacity limit (connection pool, threads, or cache memory) being hit under load and released, with no change record anywhere to support an artifact or value error [tr_ba219bb69d46, tr_c56aad5816a2, tr_f5c8228adb65]. cartservice was never dispatched, so the exhausted resource is inferred rather than observed.
verdict.reasoning: Attribution is strong, mechanism is weak. The trace evidence puts the failure boundary precisely at GetCart: 100% of traces error there, every span above it errors, and payment, email, message-publish, shipping-quote and currency-conversion spans are never entered [tr_6b9848cec352]. checkoutservice logs corroborate a silent pass-through — order initiations continue with none of the three baseline completion lines and no error-level output [tr_ba4ec2f0c565]. The flat short-baseline error ratios for frontend and checkoutservice [tr_9d797b72def0, tr_cb02d35b40c8] are consistent with a caller relaying a partial downstream failure; only the two-hour baseline exposes genuinely new error activity [tr_3c5dd3f3ddbc]. dependency_latency is excluded by the millisecond span durations [tr_6b9848cec352]. bad_config would normally fail deterministically; the recurring-burst pattern over ~80 minutes instead suggests a limit hit and released. All change queries were windowed from onset forward and returned nothing [tr_ba219bb69d46, tr_c6fd17879cf7, tr_f5c8228adb65], so they neither support nor exclude a pre-onset change.
open_questions: cartservice was never dispatched — no logs, metrics, change history or saturation signal for the service actually being blamed.
No change query covered the hours before 02:14:30; all four windows start at onset and run forward, so a pre-onset deploy or config edit remains unobserved.
The gRPC status code and error message returned by GetCart is unknown, which would distinguish resource exhaustion from a connection refusal to a wrong endpoint.

alternatives.root_cause: A configuration value in cartservice or checkoutservice points GetCart at a wrong address, port or credential, so the call fails immediately.
alternatives.why_not: A wrong endpoint or credential fails uniformly and continuously, but the error ratio is partial (~6% mean) with successful traffic throughout and three discrete crossings [tr_3c5dd3f3ddbc]; no config edit is recorded for any queried service either.

alternatives.root_cause: cartservice's backing cache/store is down or refusing connections, and cartservice fails GetCart fast as a result.
alternatives.why_not: Plausible and would produce the same trace signature, but nothing in the dispatched evidence reaches below cartservice, so it is a strictly less-supported refinement of the same blame target.

retrieved:
/ Before proposing it: A prior configuration for this service must exist in change history, and the incident's
evidence must name a configuration or flag change inside its window.

/ Confirming it: The change record shows the variable and both values. A configuration pointing at an address
that no longer answers usually produces connection errors in the service's own logs with the
address quoted verbatim - the fastest confirmation available, because the wrong value appears

/ Confirming it: Change history is the first and usually the only query needed: an image reference that changed
inside the incident window, on the service the alert names or one hop upstream of it. Logs
confirm the shape of the failure; they rarely identify it faster than the change record.

proposal.expected_effect: No action is taken, so nothing should change: checkoutservice PlaceOrder traces should continue to terminate at the CartService/GetCart ERROR span [tr_6b9848cec352] and the checkoutservice error ratio should continue its bursty pattern around a ~6% mean with peaks near 0.67 [tr_3c5dd3f3ddbc]. Before any action is proposed, three observations are needed and are all obtainable from this system: (1) cartservice logs over 00:40-02:20 to see whether GetCart is logging refusals, pool-exhaustion, or OOM lines; (2) cartservice restart-count / memory / connection metrics across the same window, which is the saturation signal the resource_exhaustion verdict currently only infers; (3) the gRPC status code on the GetCart span (RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED/UNAVAILABLE vs UNIMPLEMENTED/NOT_FOUND), which separates a capacity limit from a wrong-endpoint or contract error.
proposal.if_wrong: This abstention is wrong if cartservice is in a wedged process state that a container recreate would clear — in that case impact continues for as long as the extra diagnostics take. That cost is bounded and visible: the same error-ratio series and PlaceOrder traces already being watched would simply keep showing the failure. Conversely, the abstention is vindicated if the missing cartservice evidence shows a non-resource cause (a bad endpoint address, a code-level rejection, a dependency of cartservice such as its cache backend failing), since restart_service would not touch any of those.
proposal.risk: The named fix class is restart_service on cartservice, and restart_service is explicitly irreversible and discards in-process state. Its stated precondition is that the evidence points at process state rather than at a change; here nothing was ever collected from cartservice at all — no logs, no metrics, no change history, no saturation signal — so the precondition is asserted, not met. The verdict's own confidence is low and its shape evidence is contradictory: traces show 100% of sampled PlaceOrder calls failing uniformly [tr_6b9848cec352] while the error ratio shows partial, bursty failure with three separate crossings at 00:51, 01:20 and 02:12 [tr_3c5dd3f3ddbc], and checkoutservice logs show a silent stall with no error line naming any dependency [tr_ba4ec2f0c565]. A restart against a misdiagnosed cause destroys cartservice's in-memory carts, resets the very counters that would have identified the exhausted resource, and can produce a false recovery that is really just the next trough in an oscillating condition. rollback_image and revert_config are equally unavailable: every change query in this incident returned empty and all four windows start at onset and run forward, never covering the pre-onset hours [tr_ba219bb69d46], so no prior image tag or prior configuration is on record to restore.
proposal.blast_radius: Nobody sees a change, because nothing is changed. The ongoing impact is unchanged and already visible: frontend is the sole caller of cartservice in this incident and checkoutservice reaches it through PlaceOrder, so failed checkouts continue to surface as ERROR on frontend HTTP POST and to loadgenerator. Had the restart been proposed, its blast radius would have been cartservice for the recreate duration, with frontend and checkoutservice seeing connection resets on in-flight GetCart calls and all in-memory cart contents lost.

triage_judgement.reasoning: Critical multi-service alerting across frontend and checkout within seconds is a user-facing failure that cannot be dismissed, and no open incident could account for it. The shared downstream dependencies of both seeds are plausible but nothing in the alerts yet distinguishes a deploy, config, or dependency fault.
